title: NFCEraser: A Security Threat of NFC Message Modification Caused by Quartz Crystal Oscillator
abstract: Near Field Communication (NFC) has been widely used for rapid data exchange between electronic devices over a very short distance. In this paper, we reveal a new security vulnerability in NFC passive communication channels where transferred data can be modified in real-time. The security threat of data modification posed by this vulnerability is called NFCEraser. Exploiting electromagnetic interference (EMI), NFCEraser injects signals into the crystal oscillator's electrode and adjusts the amplitude of carrier signals in NFC communication channels. By manipulating the parameters of EMI signals, NFCEraser is able to arbitrarily flip the bits in data payload sent from an NFC peer device, which may cause serious security outcomes. To assess the severity of NFCEraser, we examine six NFC modules under NFC-A/B communication modes and successfully perform reading operations under a variety of data lengths. The experimental results show that NFCEraser can modify data bits in response frames from NFC peer devices with the maximum 89% accuracy, under around 0.21μs latency. Our analysis further shows that NFCEraser can maintain an attack success rate of no less than 85% in environments with typical levels of electromagnetic noise.

Introduction Near Field Communication (NFC) has been emerging as a prevalent communication standard in recent years. NFC is a derivative protocol of the RFID family, dependent upon RFID technology to support specific data reading and writ- ing operations for various application scenarios. It facilitates seamless communication between devices and contactless cards located nearby, usually within a few centimeters [1]. Due to its characteristics of a short transmission distance, high bandwidth, low energy consumption, and high applica- tion scalability, NFC technology has gradually been applied in numerous daily scenarios, such as electronic payment [2], attendance tracking [3], and smart advertising [4]. By the end of 2022, 85% of customers around the world have used NFC devices or contactless cards in their daily lives [5]. The NFC protocol facilitates communication between devices and cards by utilizing magnetic induction coils †Hong Li is corresponding author . E-mail: {liujianshuo,lihong,sunmengjie,wenhui,lizhi,sunlimin}@iie.ac.cn, hnw@vt.edu [1]. When an NFC reader and the user's gadgets, such as contactless cards, tags, or NFC devices, are positioned within the same magnetic field, the coils of both entities automatically establish a communication channel between them, enabling the exchange of data. The data received from NFC devices will typically be sent to upper-level applica- tions and smart devices for further processing. Despite its simplicity and convenience, NFC communication is vulner- able to malicious attacks, due to its openness and without adequate authentication and encryption mechanisms. Previ- ous research demonstrates that wireless communication data can be intercepted by malicious induction antennas [6]- [8]. Attackers can also create specific passive relay coils to intercept message transmission under a distance of up to 49.6cm [9]. More recently, attackers perform hijacking attacks by using a modified app and an auxiliary server [10]. While there has been extensive exploration of the eaves- dropping of NFC communication channels, the risk of tam- pering with the data itself has not yet been sufficiently stud- ied. Previous work [10] attempts to explore the feasibility of modifying transaction data; however, it fundamentally falls under data eavesdropping attacks and modifies the data content on the Internet rather than on the NFC communica- tion channel. Currently, the majority of NFC communication scenarios are based on the passive communication between an NFC initiator (i.e., card reader) and a peer device (e.g., a contactless card or a card simulated by a phone) [5]. The card reader is responsible for sending read and write com- mands, and the card responds with the corresponding data content. In many scenarios, such as campuses or workplaces, the data frames transmitted by a peer device (such as em- ployee ID, access records, and balances) may lack sufficient key encryption and authentication protection. Modifying the data generated by the peer device can lead to serious consequences, such as disrupting normal operations within the organization or causing financial losses to individuals. Traditionally, modifying the data content returned by the peer device is very challenging due to the characteristics of signal modulation and coupling methods. The NFC protocol employs load modulation [11] for data response, which enables the peer device to adjust the impedance of the circuit and reflect a portion of the transferred magnetic energy back to the initiator. This modulation method allows for the encoding of bit streams by modulating the carrier 2775 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00165 amplitude in the transmitted signal. It is hard to superimpose an additional magnetic field on the communication channel to modify the amplitude of the modulation signal, this is due to the nature of the peer device's energy acquisition mechanism, superimposing a magnetic field in the channel can result in unstable energy reception by the peer device, potentially causing operational abnormalities. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of NFC communication to data modification from a new perspective. Specifically, we reveal that such a vulnerability poses a real security threat to NFC applications, as adversaries can ma- nipulate the transferred data on NFC passive communication channels in real-time by addressing the challenges men- tioned above. The new and practical attack vector is to inject electromagnetic interference (EMI) signals into the quartz crystal oscillator circuit in the NFC initiator's PCB board. The quartz crystal oscillator generates stable sinusoidal sig- nals, which serve as the carrier for NFC communication. Any interruption to the output signals of the oscillator will distort the modulated signals and interfere with the signals sensed by the NFC initiator. We reveal that by injecting certain crafted signals into the oscillator, adversaries can arbitrarily modify fixed-length payload content sent by the peer device. We call such a security threat NFCEraser.I n general, NFCEraser transmits specific forms of EMI signals at specific moments according to the features of the mod- ulated signals in the communication process, to modify the specific data content (e.g., changing the ID of the employee who intends to sign out and leave the organization). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to explore the feasibility of modifying the transmission content directly in NFC peer-to-peer communication channels. We assess the security risks of NFCEraser on six off-the-shelf NFC modules with different MCU chips, under the settings of NFC-A/B communication modes, and the results show that NFCEraser can successfully modify the response frame bits with a maximum 89% success rate, and maintains desired robustness under environmental EMI noise. The major contributions of this work include: 1) We reveal a new security threat NFCEraser, which is the first real-time NFC response frame modifica- tion attack by injecting modulated electromagnetic signals into a quartz crystal oscillator. NFCEraser is able to arbitrarily flip the bit from 0 to 1 and vice versa in the fixed-length data frame. 2) We analyze the response of a crystal oscillator to EMI signals both theoretically and experimentally. We observe that the gain response of the inverting amplifier in the oscillator varies for in-band and out-of-band signals. By leveraging the response characteristics, we design principles for success- fully modifying the bits of data transmitted back by the NFC peer device. 3) We conduct the experiment to assess the security risk posed by NFCEraser on 6 off-the-shelf NFC modules with different MCU chips and propose countermeasures against this security threat. s dŽW>>ͬZ&DŽĚƵůĞ YƵĂƌƚǌƌǇƐƚĂů ĂƉĂĐŝƚŽƌ/ ĂƉĂĐŝƚŽƌ// ZĞƐŝƐƚŽƌ /Ŷǀ ĞƌƚŝŶŐ ŵƉůŝĨŝĞƌ ƵƵƵƵůĞ s dŽW>> > ͬ ͬ > > Z&DŽĚĚĚƵƵ Z& Z ZĞƐŝƐƚŽ Ž Žƌ /ŶǀĞƌƚŝŶŐ ŵƉůŝĨŝĞƌ Ɖ /ŶƐŝĚĞDh KƵƚƐŝĚĞD h sƐƐ Figure 1. Section 3 presents the threat model, including the attack goal, a common attack scenario, and attack assumptions. Section 4 shows the de- tailed methods to modify the amplitude of carrier signal, and Section 5 details the attack steps. Section 6 evaluates the performance of NFCEraser. Section 7 discusses the limitations and countermeasures of the threat. Section 8 surveys the related work on NFC and EMI-related attacks, and finally Section 9 concludes the work. 2. Background In this section, we present the composition and op- erational logic of the quartz crystal oscillator and NFC communication module. 2.1. Quartz Crystal Oscillator The quartz crystal oscillator is a frequency-selective circuit that utilizes a quartz crystal as its core component [12]. The quartz crystal possesses a significant property called the Piezoelectric effect [13], wherein it undergoes periodic compression or stretching of its volume when sub- jected to an alternating electric field. The variation in crystal volume induces charges on its surface to counterbalance the deformation, thus forming the alternating signal in the circuit. Owing to its high quality factor [14] and minimal frequency deviation caused by temperature fluctuations in its surroundings, the quartz crystal oscillator offers superior ac- curacy and stability compared to other oscillation modules, such as the CMOS oscillator [15]. Consequently, the quartz crystal oscillator has widespread use in electronic circuits for generating reliable reference signals. The reference signal can be utilized in various applications. After passing through the phase-locked loop (PLL) [16], it can serve as the system clock signal in an IC chip [17]; when passing through the radio-frequency mixer [18], the reference signal can be employed as an RF carrier [19]. In an oscillator circuit, the quartz crystal is commonly used as the inductive element. Section 7 discusses the limitations and countermeasures of the threat. Section 8 surveys the related work on NFC and EMI-related attacks, and finally Section 9 concludes the work. 2. Background In this section, we present the composition and op- erational logic of the quartz crystal oscillator and NFC communication module. 2.1. Quartz Crystal Oscillator The quartz crystal oscillator is a frequency-selective circuit that utilizes a quartz crystal as its core component [12]. The quartz crystal possesses a significant property called the Piezoelectric effect [13], wherein it undergoes periodic compression or stretching of its volume when sub- jected to an alternating electric field. The variation in crystal volume induces charges on its surface to counterbalance the deformation, thus forming the alternating signal in the circuit. Owing to its high quality factor [14] and minimal frequency deviation caused by temperature fluctuations in its surroundings, the quartz crystal oscillator offers superior ac- curacy and stability compared to other oscillation modules, such as the CMOS oscillator [15]. Consequently, the quartz crystal oscillator has widespread use in electronic circuits for generating reliable reference signals. The reference signal can be utilized in various applications. After passing through the phase-locked loop (PLL) [16], it can serve as the system clock signal in an IC chip [17]; when passing through the radio-frequency mixer [18], the reference signal can be employed as an RF carrier [19]. In an oscillator circuit, the quartz crystal is commonly used as the inductive element. The Pierce oscillator [20] has been widely used as the preferred configuration for the quartz crystal oscillator circuit, as shown in Fig. 1. Two 2776

Near Field Communication (NFC) has been widely used for rapid data exchange between electronic devices over a very short distance. In this paper, we reveal a new security vulnerability in NFC passive communication channels where transferred data can be modified in real-time. The security threat of data modification posed by this vulnerability is called NFCEraser. Exploiting electromagnetic interference (EMI), NFCEraser injects signals into the crystal oscillator's electrode and adjusts the amplitude of carrier signals in NFC communication channels. By manipulating the parameters of EMI signals, NFCEraser is able to arbitrarily flip the bits in data payload sent from an NFC peer device, which may cause serious security outcomes. To assess the severity of NFCEraser, we examine six NFC modules under NFC-A/B communication modes and successfully perform reading operations under a variety of data lengths. The experimental results show that NFCEraser can modify data bits in response frames from NFC peer devices with the maximum 89% accuracy, under around 0.21μs latency. Our analysis further shows that NFCEraser can maintain an attack success rate of no less than 85% in environments with typical levels of electromagnetic noise.
